what.a: Open this computer's terminals from your phone or any browser: see how Claude Code or Codex is doing and reply to keep it going; run commands and read logs too. Close the page and tasks keep running.

vs.q: Is it like remote control tools such as ToDesk?
vs.a: No. ToDesk streams the whole desktop, which suits graphical apps; Looklook opens only the terminal, built for the command line and AI coding assistants.

better.q: How is it better than remote desktop?
better.a: Text is sharp on a phone and typing works normally, with an Esc/Ctrl key bar. Only text is sent, so it uses little data and stays smooth on poor signal; the computer can be locked, and servers and NAS work too. For graphical desktop work, remote desktop is the better fit.

install.q: Do I install it on both the computer and phone?
install.a: Only this computer needs Looklook (the one you're using now). Phones and other computers need nothing: open your personal address in a browser and sign in.

safety.title: Security notice
safety.body: The Looklook dashboard uses port {{port}} on this computer. If this computer has a public IP (e.g. a cloud server), do not open port {{port}} to the internet in the firewall, security group or router. To connect from outside, use your personal address (requires signing in to Looklook).

safety.open_no_code: Devices on the LAN or allowlist may open the dashboard, but no access code is enabled: anyone on the same network can open your terminals. Enable the access code in Settings → Access control.

access.title: Access control
access.intro: This computer can always open the dashboard itself. Here you decide whether other devices can connect directly to it. To use it from your phone outside, use your personal address; no change is needed here.
access.lan: Allow devices on the LAN to open it
access.lan_hint: When on, phones and computers on the same Wi‑Fi or router can open the dashboard by entering this computer's LAN address (e.g. http://192.168.1.20:1234) in a browser. Useful when Looklook runs on a NAS or another computer at home. Don't enable it on shared networks such as cafés or offices. If unsure, leave it off.
access.lan_urls: Devices on the LAN open this address:
access.lan_unknown: Couldn't find this computer's LAN address. Check its IP in your router's admin page, then open http://that-IP:{{port}}/
access.lan_no_code: Also enable the access code, otherwise anyone on the same Wi‑Fi can open your terminals.
access.code_hint: The access code is stored only on this computer (in Looklook's local database) and is never uploaded to the Looklook server. When on, devices on the LAN or allowlist must enter it the first time they open the dashboard, and that browser remembers it for 30 days; this computer itself doesn't need it. Purpose: stop other people on the same network from opening your terminals.
access.code_forgot: After changing the code, browsers that entered the old one must enter it again. Forgot it? Open this page on this computer to view it, or run looklook access in a terminal. 10 wrong attempts lock you out for 15 minutes.
access.list_hint: Usually not needed. Add an entry only to open the dashboard directly from another network (e.g. an office): a single IP, a range or a domain, such as 203.0.113.7, 203.0.113.0/24 or home.example.com. If that network has a dynamic public IP, enter its DDNS domain: Looklook resolves it regularly and lets in visitors whose IP matches. Enabling the access code is recommended when using the allowlist.
access.list_no_code: IPs on the allowlist can currently open the dashboard without an access code; enabling the access code is recommended.
access.open_host_hint: The address Looklook opens in the browser at startup. If Looklook runs on a NAS or server and you usually open it from another computer on the LAN, enter that machine's IP or domain; host only, without http:// or a port. When using a domain, that domain is also allowed. Leave empty for this computer.
access.remote_only: Access control can't be changed when opened through the personal address. Change it on this computer or on an allowed LAN device.
access.fw_title: Windows showed "Windows Defender Firewall has blocked some features of this app"?
access.fw_why: The Looklook dashboard listens on all network adapters so you can allow LAN access when needed, so Windows asks on first run whether to allow it. This isn't a virus warning; choose according to how you use it:
access.fw_local: Only using it on this computer: click "Cancel". This computer opens it as usual, and using your personal address from your phone outside is unaffected.
access.fw_lan: To let other devices at home open it: tick only "Private networks" and click "Allow access". Don't tick "Public networks" (cafés, airports, etc.).
access.fw_profile: Allowed but still can't connect: in Windows Settings → Network & Internet → Wi‑Fi (or Ethernet) → your network, set the network profile type to "Private".
access.fw_fix: Clicked the wrong option and want to change it: open Control Panel → Windows Defender Firewall → Allow an app through Windows Firewall → Change settings, find looklook and tick only "Private". You can also run this in PowerShell as administrator:
access.fw_never: To never see this prompt: set the environment variable LOOKLOOK_LISTEN=127.0.0.1:1234 and reopen Looklook. Then the dashboard can only be opened on this computer, and LAN access won't work.
access.lan_switch: Offer the local network when opened remotely
access.lan_switch_hint: When you open Looklook remotely with your account while on the same network as this computer (say, your phone at home), the page offers a faster direct connection over the local network. Only browsers signed in to your account can switch; it doesn't need "Allow LAN" above or the access code.

state.connected: Remote tunnel connected — phones and other computers can open this
state.blocked: Remote tunnel connected, but the remote console can't connect

relay.local_ok: Using terminals on this computer is not affected; you just can't open them remotely from a phone or another computer for now. Looklook keeps retrying automatically.
relay.blocked_why: This computer can't reach UDP port 3478 on route {{name}}. The remote console sets up its encrypted connection over UDP, so opening it from a phone or another computer will fail. Usually the network (office, school, some cloud servers) blocks UDP.
relay.blocked_fix: Using it on this computer is not affected. Try another network (such as a phone hotspot), or switch to a route that shows a latency:

reason.dns: Can't find the Looklook server's address (DNS lookup failed). Check this computer's network, or switch DNS (e.g. 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
reason.refused: The server refused the connection. It may be under maintenance or blocked by a firewall; Looklook will retry shortly.
reason.timeout: Connecting to the server timed out. Check that your network works; office or school networks sometimes block this kind of connection, so try a phone hotspot.
reason.network: The network is unreachable. Make sure this computer is connected to the internet.
reason.auth: The server didn't accept this computer's credentials. Sign out on the Account page and sign in again.
reason.handshake: The encrypted handshake with the server failed. Usually the network is interfering, or Looklook is too old — please update to the latest version.
reason.heartbeat: The connection to the server dropped (no response for a long time). Reconnecting automatically.
reason.config: Couldn't write the remote access configuration. Check disk space and file permissions.
reason.other: Something went wrong connecting to the server; Looklook will retry. If it keeps failing, expand the technical details and send them to us.

relay.auto_note: Reconnects right away when this computer wakes up or changes networks, and keeps retrying if the link drops.

relays.title: Remote route
relays.intro: When you open this computer from your phone or another computer, the data goes through a Looklook route. Looklook tests the routes regularly and uses the one with the lowest latency, so you usually don't need to do anything.
relays.when_slow: If remote access feels laggy or typing is delayed, pick a route with lower latency below. Once you pick one yourself it won't switch automatically, and Looklook remembers your choice. If a route gets noticeably slow, you'll see a reminder at the top of the page.
relays.auto_hint: This computer tests the routes regularly and uses the one with the lowest latency. It only switches when no terminal is open, and moves to another route if one fails
relays.measuring: Testing speed, this takes a few seconds…

relays.fallback: The route you chose ({{preferred}}) isn't available right now, so {{current}} is being used for the moment. It switches back automatically once {{preferred}} recovers.
relays.latency_explain: Latency is how long data takes to travel from this computer to the route and back. Lower is faster. When a browser can't reach this computer directly, remote access relays through the route along this same path. "Can't connect" means UDP between this computer and the route is blocked, so with that route remote access only works on the same local network.
relays.switch_note: Switching routes disconnects any open remote pages for a few seconds, then they reconnect on their own. Your personal address stays the same.
relays.hint_now: Remote access is a bit slow: your current route {{name}} takes about {{ms}} ms,
relays.hint_now_down: Remote access is a bit slow: your current route {{name}} isn't responding,
relays.hint_better: while route {{name}} takes only about {{ms}} ms.

model.title: Model providers
model.intro: Route Claude Code and Codex through a third-party API (relay or aggregator) and pay the provider with an API key. Without one, the official API and your own sign-in are used.
model.reset_title: Switch {{agent}} back to the official API?
model.reset_body: The API key saved on this computer will be deleted. Running terminals are not affected until they restart.
model.reset_done: Back to the official API. Restart terminals to apply.
model.restart_note: Applies to terminals created or restarted afterwards; running terminals keep their current API.
model.custom_desc: Enter an endpoint from another provider
model.custom_url_hint_claude: The provider's Anthropic-compatible URL (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL). Must be https.
model.custom_url_hint_codex: The provider's OpenAI Responses-compatible URL, usually ending in /v1. Must be https.
model.none: No recommended providers yet. Choose “Custom” to enter an endpoint.
model.list_failed: Couldn't load the recommended list (server unreachable). You can use “Custom” for now.
model.key_hint: Create it on the provider's website. It stays on this computer and is never uploaded to Looklook.
model.key_keep: Leave empty to keep the saved key. Enter a new one if you switched providers.
model.saved: Provider for {{agent}} saved. Applies to new or restarted terminals.

disclaimer.title: Disclaimer: third-party services are provided by the providers
disclaimer.third_party: Providers in this list are run by third parties; items marked “Ad” are sponsored. Looklook does not provide or operate these services and makes no guarantee of their availability, stability, security, model authenticity or compliance.
disclaimer.data: Once enabled, your conversations with the AI, code and file contents in the terminal are sent directly to the provider you choose. Judge their trustworthiness yourself and don't use them for sensitive or confidential data.
disclaimer.key: Your API key stays on this computer; Looklook never uploads or reads it. Keep it safe and revoke it with the provider if it leaks.
disclaimer.cost: Charges, top-ups, refunds and support are between you and the provider. Looklook is not liable for costs, data leaks, account actions or other losses arising from third-party services. You must also follow the model vendor's terms and local laws.
disclaimer.agree: I have read and agree to the above, and use third-party services at my own risk

ssh.title: SSH hosts
ssh.delete_body: This only removes the host and its saved password and uploaded key from Looklook. The server and your keys in ~/.ssh are untouched.
ssh.name: Name
ssh.name_hint: For you — AI assistants also use it to pick the host.

auth_hint.agent: Uses this computer’s default keys in ~/.ssh or ssh-agent, exactly like running ssh in a terminal. Looklook stores no secrets.
auth_hint.key: Sign in with a private key: pick a key file on this computer (Looklook keeps the path only) or upload one from your browser (stored encrypted). A passphrase can be stored too.
auth_hint.password: The password is encrypted on this computer and handed to ssh by Looklook when connecting. It’s never shown and never appears in the terminal.
auth_hint.jump: Signs in to the jump host first, then runs ssh from there to this host using the keys already set up on the jump host (its ~/.ssh or ssh-agent). No password or key needed here.

ssh.key_path_hint: A path on this computer (~ means your home folder), or click Browse to pick the file.
ssh.secret_saved: Saved encrypted. Leave blank to keep it.
ssh.secret_hint: Encrypted and kept on this computer only — never uploaded to Looklook’s servers.
ssh.allow_ai: Let AI assistants use this host
ssh.allow_ai_hint: When on, Claude Code, Codex and others can run commands on this host through Looklook's MCP interface. Looklook signs in for them; they never see the password or key, and passwords, keys and common tokens are removed from the output. See and switch all AI tools on the AI assistants page.
ssh.empty_body: Save the servers you use: open an SSH terminal in one click without typing passwords, and optionally let AI assistants run commands there safely.
ssh.no_ssh: No ssh command found on this computer. Install the OpenSSH client first (Windows: Settings → Optional features → OpenSSH Client).
ssh.safety_1: Passwords, key passphrases and uploaded keys are encrypted with a key on this computer and kept in Looklook’s database — never uploaded to Looklook’s servers.
ssh.safety_2: When connecting, ssh asks Looklook for the password through SSH_ASKPASS over a one-time local channel — it never appears in command lines, environment variables, files or terminal output.
ssh.safety_3: AI assistants can only use hosts with "Let AI assistants use" on, and only once the MCP interface is on:
ssh.safety_4: Limits: AI assistants run as the same system user as Looklook and can read any file you can (including ~/.ssh). This keeps passwords out of chats, logs and screenshots; don’t run untrusted programs on this computer.
ssh.key_upload_hint: The key is encrypted and kept in Looklook’s database on this computer — never uploaded to Looklook’s servers. When connecting it’s written to a file only you can read and deleted once ssh has read it. OpenSSH / PEM format only.
ssh.key_read_failed: Couldn’t read that file (too large or not a text file)
ssh.ki_no_fp: (PEM key without a .pub file next to it — fingerprint unavailable)
ssh.sys_intro: ssh will try these keys in order when connecting (plus any IdentityFile set for this host in ~/.ssh/config). Contents are masked.
ssh.sys_agent_off: Couldn’t reach ssh-agent (not running, or ssh-add isn’t installed).
ssh.sys_agent_empty: ssh-agent is running but holds no keys.
ssh.sys_files_empty: No default keys such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 or id_rsa were found.
ssh.jump_auth_tip: Is this host’s key set up on the jump host, so you can ssh to it from there?
ssh.jump_hint: If this host can’t be reached directly, connect to a jump host first (another SSH host) and go on from there.
ssh.jump_no_hosts: There are no other hosts to use as a jump host yet. Choose “New jump host”.
ssh.jump_new_note: Saving also creates a new SSH host “{{name}}” as the jump host. It shows up in your host list, where you can connect to it, edit it, or use it as the jump host for other hosts.
ssh.jump_created: Also created the jump host “{{name}}”; “{{host}}” connects through it
ssh.jump_via_hint: Connects to this jump host first, then on to this host
ssh.test_stale: The form has changed; this result is from before the change.
ssh.diag_via: This host is reached through the jump host "{{via}}": the jump host itself may be unreachable, or it may not be able to reach this host. Try testing the jump host first.

diag_win.password: This is a Windows server: use the Windows account name (a PC signed in with a Microsoft account may need the email address; a domain account needs DOMAIN\user). The password is the Windows sign-in password, not the PIN.
diag_win.key: This is a Windows server: if the account is in the Administrators group, the public key must go in C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys (accessible only to SYSTEM and Administrators), not in .ssh\authorized_keys in the user folder.
diag_win.shell: This is a Windows server: the default shell is cmd or PowerShell, not bash, so Linux commands won't run there.

unknown.title: Connection failed
unknown.hint: The exact cause wasn't recognized. See the error message and full log below.

dns.title: Address not found
dns.hint: This computer can't resolve the host name. Check the spelling, or whether the name only resolves inside a private network or VPN.

refused.title: Connection refused
refused.hint: Nothing is listening on this port of {{target}}. Check the port, whether sshd is running (Windows: the OpenSSH SSH Server service), and whether a firewall rejects it.

timeout.title: No response
timeout.hint: {{target}} never answered. Usually a firewall or security group blocks the port, the address is wrong, or you need a VPN or jump host first.

unreachable.title: Network unreachable
unreachable.hint: There is no route to {{target}}. The host is on a different network; you may need a VPN or a jump host.

closed.title: The server closed the connection
closed.hint: The TCP connection opened but was closed before sign-in. The port may not be SSH, or the server blocks your IP (fail2ban, allow lists, connection limits).

hostkey_changed.title: The server's identity changed
hostkey_changed.hint: The host key of {{target}} differs from the one in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. The server may have been reinstalled or its IP reassigned, or the connection may be intercepted. Once you've confirmed the change is expected, run ssh-keygen -R <host> to remove the old entry.

algo.title: No common algorithms
algo.hint: This computer's ssh and the server share no supported algorithm (common with very old servers or devices). Upgrade the server's OpenSSH or allow legacy algorithms for it in ~/.ssh/config.

auth_method.title: The server doesn't allow this sign-in method
auth_method.hint: The server doesn't accept the method you chose. See the methods it accepts below and switch (e.g. use a private key if it only accepts publickey).

auth_password.title: Wrong password, or password sign-in not allowed for this user
auth_password.hint: The server rejected the password for {{target}}. Check the user name and password; some servers forbid password sign-in for root (PermitRootLogin) or only allow it for some users.

auth_key.title: The server doesn't accept this key
auth_key.hint: The matching public key isn't in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for this user on the server, or the user name is wrong.

auth_agent.title: All system keys were rejected
auth_agent.hint: ssh tried {{n}} key(s) from this computer and the server accepted none. Add one of their public keys to the server's authorized_keys, or switch to a specific key or a password.

no_keys.title: No keys on this computer
no_keys.hint: "System keys" is selected, but neither ssh-agent nor ~/.ssh has a key to try. Use a private key (upload or pick a file) or a password.

jump_inner.title: The jump host can't sign in to the target
jump_inner.hint: Connected to the jump host "{{via}}", but ssh from there to {{target}} was rejected. The jump host user's key isn't on the target, or a password is required (sign-in via jump host can't enter passwords).

key_missing.title: Key file not found
key_missing.hint: The key file doesn't exist or can't be read. Check the path.

key_perms.title: Key file permissions are wrong
key_perms.hint: ssh only uses a key file that only you can read: run chmod 600 on it (on Windows, remove other users' access to it).

key_format.title: Key format not recognized
key_format.hint: ssh can't read this key file. It may be a PuTTY .ppk (export it as OpenSSH from PuTTYgen first) or damaged.

passphrase.title: Wrong key passphrase
passphrase.hint: The key is passphrase-protected and the saved passphrase doesn't unlock it. Edit the host and enter the passphrase again.

askpass.title: Couldn't hand the password to ssh
askpass.hint: This computer's ssh didn't ask Looklook for the password (OpenSSH may be too old to support SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE). Upgrade the OpenSSH client or use a private key.

auth_timeout.title: Sign-in got stuck
auth_timeout.hint: Connected, but sign-in never finished. The server may require extra verification (two-factor, a code) or be waiting for input. For now, sign in to such hosts by hand in an SSH terminal.

sftp_only.title: This account is SFTP-only
sftp_only.hint: Signed in, but the server only lets this account transfer files (ForceCommand internal-sftp); it can't run commands.

remote_cmd.title: Signed in, but the command failed
remote_cmd.hint: Signed in to {{target}}, but the remote shell failed to run the test command (exit code {{code}}). The account's shell may be nologin, or the server restricts commands.

remote_output.title: Signed in, but the output was unexpected
remote_output.hint: Signed in to {{target}} and the command finished, but the expected output didn't appear. The server may use ForceCommand, or a login script swallows output.

command_timeout.title: Signed in, but the command never finished
command_timeout.hint: Signed in, but the test command hadn't finished after 25 seconds. A login script (.bashrc etc.) may be waiting for input.

ai.title: AI tools & access
ai.intro: AI assistants such as Claude Code and Codex use Looklook through its MCP interface. Set the interface up here and see and control what they can do.
ai.local_only: The MCP token and installation can only be viewed and changed when the console is opened directly on this computer. The host switches below also work remotely.
ai.tools_intro: The MCP interface is on; AI assistants can use the tools that are on below.
ai.tools_off: The MCP interface is off, so AI assistants can't use any tools right now. The tools below apply once it is on.
ai.ssh_switch: Let AI assistants use SSH hosts
ai.ssh_on_hint: AI assistants can only use the hosts switched on below. Looklook signs in for them; they never see passwords or keys, and passwords, keys and common tokens are removed from the output.
ai.ssh_off_hint: Off: AI assistants don't see the SSH tools and can't run commands on any host. The per-host switches below are kept for when you turn this back on.
ai.ssh_switch_local: This master switch can only be changed when the console is opened directly on this computer.
ai.no_hosts: No SSH hosts saved yet. Add one:
